newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico soybean imports continue at brisk pace.
newsitem.headline: Mexico soybean imports continue at brisk pace.

text.p: Mexico is importing soybeans at a brisk pace largely because of weak domestic output and the high price fetched by local soybean meal, sources said.
To Nov 20, imports in the marketing year Sept 1-Aug 31 had totaled 503,000 tonnes versus 480,500 tonnes a cycle earlier, the local office of the American Soybean Association (ASA) said in an update.
That import rhythm makes Mexico on line to buy this calendar year far above the 2.2 million tonnes brought into the country in the 1995.
ASA upgraded its prediction for imports in 1996 to close to 3 million tonnes from a previous estimate that it would "top 2.8 million tonnes".
"The lack of a domestic crop is still forcing good volumes of U.S. soybeans to be imported," a local trader said.

Gonzalo Cardenas Jimenez, chairman of the Chamber of Western Edible Oil Manufacturers, told Reuters recently his estimate was for output to drop in 1996 to just 50,000 tonnes from 135,000 tonnes in 1995.
Mexican production has been on the wane since a 1989 peak of 942,000 tonnes, mainly because of sporadic droughts.

"Some of the grains traders dealing in Mexico report a very brisk demand for soybeans in Mexico," ASA said. "Some of larger crushers such as Agydsa and Gamesa were in the market for large quantities (last week)," it added.
Also, reports suggest that smaller crushers along Mexico's Pacific coast, in the states of Sonora and Sinaloa, are also increasing import quantities.
One of the reasons for this strong pace of imports is the high local price of soybean meal, the ASA said. "Oil prices have been steady so crushers are working on high margins at this time," it added.

Even the promotion of safflower plantings in states such as Jalisco is no denting the import surge, sources said. Jalisco has promoted more plantings of the unfashionable but high-yield oilseed as an alternative, especially to soybeans.

National safflower output is seen ending at 150,000 tonnes this calendar year, up from the 80,000 tonnes of 1995, but still a far cry from the 480,000 tonnes produced in 1980, according to the Agriculture Ministry.
But despite the hike in output, the soybean trade is not nervous about the safflower surge because of the production numbers are still relatively low.
"Nobody thinks this movement for safflower poses a threat to soybeans," ASA said.

Delays in the imports of other grains, such as sorghum, point toward the ASA's increased import prediction, another trader said. He added there were no railcar shortages, seaports were not congested and credits were operative.
"December should be a good month for soybean imports, bringing the total for the year very close to the 3 million tonne mark," the ASA said.
